# Introduction

This report documents the data preparation process for Case 31: Employees Federal Credit Union (EFCU).

The purpose is to prepare survey responses for statistical analysis by examining variable labels, measurement scales, missing values, and response coding.

The preparation process follows Professor Jung's Case 31 workshop and uses R and Quarto to create a reproducible report.

# Importing the Dataset

## Loading Required Packages

```{r}
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
```

## Reading the SPSS Data

```{r}
case31 <- read_sav("data/Case 31 Data_efcu_1.sav")

dim(case31)
names(case31)
```

## Initial Data Inspection

```{r}
head(case31)
summary(case31)
```

# Creating a Data Dictionary

A data dictionary helps researchers understand the meaning of each variable, its data type, and its response categories.

The Case 31 questionnaire provides the original questions and coding information needed to interpret the dataset correctly.

```{r}
library(labelled)

data_dictionary <- labelled::look_for(case31)

data_dictionary
```

# Measurement Scales

Understanding measurement scales is important because the type of variable determines which statistical methods are appropriate.

## Ordinal Variables

Ordinal variables contain categories with a meaningful order.

In Case 31, questions Q3–Q6 measure employee service characteristics using a five-point agreement scale.

Questions Q7–Q8 and Q37 also use ordered response categories.

## Nominal Variables

Nominal variables represent categories without a meaningful numerical ranking.

For example, Q27 identifies whether a member currently has a loan with the credit union, while Q38 identifies whether the respondent lives in the headquarters area.

## Examining Variable Labels

```{r}
haven::as_factor(case31$q3) |> table(useNA = "ifany")

haven::as_factor(case31$q7) |> table(useNA = "ifany")

haven::as_factor(case31$q37) |> table(useNA = "ifany")

haven::as_factor(case31$q38) |> table(useNA = "ifany")
```

These frequency tables help verify that the numerical values correspond to the correct response categories.

## Reflection

I learned that identifying measurement scales is an important part of preparing survey data. Although Likert-scale responses are stored as numbers, they represent ordered categories rather than continuous measurements.

Understanding these differences helps researchers select appropriate analytical techniques and avoid misinterpreting survey responses.

# Checking Missing Values

Before recoding variables, I examined missing responses and special response codes to determine which values should be retained or treated as missing.

## Missing Values by Variable

```{r}
missing_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(case31),
  Missing = sapply(case31, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
)

missing_summary
```

## Checking Special Response Codes

```{r}
table(case31$q7, useNA = "ifany")
table(case31$q8, useNA = "ifany")
table(case31$q37, useNA = "ifany")
```

These tables help identify missing values and response categories that may require recoding before analysis.

# Preparing a Cleaned Dataset

The original SPSS dataset is preserved to maintain data integrity. A separate working copy is created for cleaning and recoding.

## Creating a Working Copy

```{r}
case31_clean <- case31

dim(case31_clean)
```

## Reviewing Special Response Codes

```{r}
table(case31_clean$q7, useNA = "ifany")
table(case31_clean$q8, useNA = "ifany")
table(case31_clean$q37, useNA = "ifany")
```

The questionnaire identifies special response categories that must be distinguished from valid ratings before analysis.

# Verifying Response Codes

The questionnaire uses different numerical coding schemes. I checked the observed values before recoding to avoid changing valid responses.

```{r}
variables_to_check <- c(
  "q3", "q4", "q5", "q6",
  "q7", "q8",
  "q30", "q31", "q32", "q33", "q34",
  "q37"
)

lapply(case31_clean[variables_to_check], function(x) {
  table(as.numeric(x), useNA = "ifany")
})
```

# Recoding Survey Variables

The Case 31 questionnaire uses different response scales. Some variables require reverse coding to make their direction easier to interpret.

The original variables are preserved, and new variables are created for analysis.

## Reverse Coding Interest Rate Evaluations

```{r}
case31_clean <- case31_clean |>
  mutate(
    q7_reverse = 6 - as.numeric(q7),
    q8_reverse = 6 - as.numeric(q8)
  )

summary(case31_clean[, c("q7_reverse", "q8_reverse")])
```

The reversed variables range from 1 to 5, with higher values representing perceptions of lower interest rates.

Missing values remain missing.

## Reverse Coding Overall Evaluation

```{r}
case31_clean <- case31_clean |>
  mutate(
    q37_reverse = 6 - as.numeric(q37)
  )

table(case31_clean$q37_reverse, useNA = "ifany")
```

The reversed overall evaluation variable ranges from 1 to 5, where higher scores indicate more favorable evaluations of the credit union.

## Reflection

This process demonstrated why researchers must examine the original questionnaire before recoding variables.

Although the survey responses are stored numerically, the direction and meaning of the scales differ across questions.

Creating separate reversed variables preserves the original responses while making subsequent analysis easier to interpret.

# Evaluating Employee Proficiency and Operational Efficiency

The Case 31 questionnaire contains multiple questions related to employee performance and credit union operations.

Before creating composite measures, I examined the relationships among the survey items.

## Employee Proficiency

Questions Q3–Q6 measure employee courtesy, helpfulness, professionalism, and availability.

```{r}
employee_items <- case31_clean |>
  select(q3, q4, q5, q6) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

cor(employee_items, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
```

## Operational Efficiency

Questions Q30–Q34 measure different aspects of credit union operations.

```{r}
operations_items <- case31_clean |>
  select(q30, q31, q32, q33, q34) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

cor(operations_items, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
```

## Interpretation

Correlation analysis helps determine whether survey items are related enough to consider combining them into composite measures.

Strong positive correlations suggest that items may reflect a common underlying concept. However, correlation alone does not establish reliability or construct validity.

Further evaluation is necessary before deciding whether all items should be combined.

# Reliability Analysis

Cronbach's alpha was used to examine the internal consistency of the survey items measuring employee proficiency and operational efficiency.

## Employee Proficiency Reliability

```{r}
library(psych)

employee_alpha <- psych::alpha(employee_items)

employee_alpha$total$raw_alpha
```

## Operational Efficiency Reliability

```{r}
operations_alpha <- psych::alpha(operations_items)

operations_alpha$total$raw_alpha
```

## Interpretation

Cronbach's alpha helps determine whether multiple survey items consistently measure a related concept.

Values around 0.70 or higher are commonly considered acceptable for exploratory research, although the appropriate threshold depends on the research context.

The reliability results will help determine whether composite measures are appropriate for the Case 31 dataset.

## Operational Efficiency Item Analysis

The operational efficiency scale showed relatively low internal consistency. I examined how Cronbach's alpha would change if individual items were removed.

```{r}
operations_alpha$alpha.drop
```

# Creating Composite Measures

## Employee Proficiency Composite

The four employee proficiency items demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.866).

Therefore, I created a composite score using the average of Q3–Q6.

```{r}
case31_clean$employee_proficiency <- rowMeans(
  case31_clean[, c("q3", "q4", "q5", "q6")],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

summary(case31_clean$employee_proficiency)
```

Higher composite scores indicate more favorable perceptions of employee courtesy, helpfulness, professionalism, and availability.

## Operational Efficiency Decision

The five operational efficiency items demonstrated low internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.539).

Removing individual items did not improve reliability. Therefore, I retained Q30–Q34 as separate variables rather than creating a combined operational efficiency index.

This decision preserves the individual information provided by each survey question and avoids combining items that may represent different aspects of credit union operations.

# Saving the Cleaned Dataset

## Labelling the Composite Variable

The employee proficiency composite represents the average rating of employee courtesy, helpfulness, professionalism, and availability.

```{r}
labelled::var_label(case31_clean$employee_proficiency) <-
  "Employee Proficiency Composite (Q3-Q6)"

labelled::var_label(case31_clean$employee_proficiency)
```

## Exporting the Prepared Data

The cleaned dataset is saved separately from the original SPSS file to preserve the raw responses.

```{r}
haven::write_sav(
  case31_clean,
  "data/Case31-Cleaned.sav"
)

dim(case31_clean)
```

The exported dataset retains the original survey variables and includes the newly created variables for subsequent analysis.

# Conclusion

This assignment helped me understand the importance of preparing survey data before conducting statistical analysis.

Using R and Quarto, I imported the Case 31 SPSS dataset, examined variable labels and measurement scales, identified missing values, and created reverse-coded variables.

I also evaluated the reliability of two proposed constructs: Employee Proficiency and Operational Efficiency.

The Employee Proficiency scale demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.866), supporting the creation of a composite score. The average Employee Proficiency rating was 4.21 out of 5.

In contrast, Operational Efficiency demonstrated lower internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.539). Therefore, I retained its original items rather than combining them into a single index.

The prepared dataset was exported as a separate SPSS file to preserve the original responses and support future analysis.
